You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Strait of Hormuz News Today: US-Iran Conflict Timeline, Oil Prices, Gold Trends and CFD Trading

TEXT:
July 15: President Trump said the ceasefire with Iran has “ended” and warned of military consequences if Iran fails to keep all routes in the Strait of Hormuz fully open.
Market Reaction: Brent crude saw a sharp rebound from oversold levels.
Read More: Brent Crude: Geopolitical Short Squeeze Hits Major Resistance
July 1: U.S. negotiators refused direct talks with Iran in Doha over a proposed transit-fee system near the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint for nearly 20% of global energy supply.
Market Reaction: Silver faced heavy selling pressure and broke below the key $58 level.
Read More: XAG/USD Deep Dive: U.S.-Iran Tensions and the NFP Shock
June 9, after a U.S. Apache helicopter crashed in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. and Iran quickly entered a cycle of tit-for-tat military retaliation. Yet while air-raid sirens sounded and missiles crossed the night sky, the White House continued to send dovish signals that a nuclear deal could be close.
Market reaction: Bullish for crude oil; Nasdaq sold off sharply.
Read more: The Brink of War and Nuclear Talks: How the US-Iran Conflict is Shaking Global Trading Assets
June 1, Iranian media reports Iran and the "Resistance Front" plan to fully blockade the Strait of Hormuz and expand operations to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Meanwhile, indirect talks with the US via mediators are tentatively planned.
Market Reaction: Oil prices skyrocketed. Brent crude surged nearly 6% and WTI spiked over 7% in a single day.
Read more: War Reignites in the Middle East! Crude Oil Surges, Safe-Haven Sentiment Soars—What should CFD traders pay attention to?
May 28, reports said U.S. and Iranian negotiators had agreed on a framework for a 60-day memorandum of understanding to extend the ceasefire and start talks on Iran’s nuclear issue, pending final approval from President Trump. Iran denied the reports. A new round of U.S.–Iran military clashes occurred the same day.
Market reaction: Nasdaq hit a record high. Oil pulled back, while gold and silver saw increased volatility.
Read more: US Nasdaq Hits All-Time High! Latest on the Middle East: How Are Oil, Gold, Silver, and Nasdaq CFD Trends Affected?
May 24 — Rubio said U.S.–Iran talks made major progress in the past 48 hours, with a draft deal backed by 7–8 Middle Eastern countries. Trump said talks were “orderly and constructive” and told negotiators not to rush.
Market reaction: Iran–Israel tensions eased; crude oil fell nearly 6% on May 25.
Read more: Middle East Tensions Ease: Is Crude Oil CFD Still a Buy? UKOUSD Outlook
May 17 — Israeli media said Netanyahu and Trump discussed restarting military action against Iran.
Market reaction: Conflict risks rose; oil strengthened on supply concerns.
Read more: Iran–Israel Tensions May Resume: How to Trade Crude Oil CFD? UKOUSD Outlook
May 15 — Trump said he did not initially support the U.S.–Iran ceasefire, while Iran said the U.S. rejected its 14-point peace proposal.
Market reaction: Oil surged; gold fell.
May 10 — Two tankers carrying about 2M barrels of crude crossed the Strait of Hormuz. Iran set five conditions for new U.S.–Iran talks, while Trump called Iran’s ceasefire proposal “unacceptable.”
Market reaction: Talks stalled; Hormuz closure risks kept oil prices elevated.
Read more：What Are the Differences Between West Texas Intermediate (USOUSD) and Brent Crude (UKOUSD)?
May 2 — Iran disclosed a 14-point proposal focused on ending the war, while the U.S. had proposed a two-month ceasefire.
Market reaction: After the May 4 open, oil rose about 5% on risk premium; safe-haven assets weakened.
April 22 - Iranian media and the country's UN representative confirm that clear signals have been received from the U.S. about its readiness to "end the blockade."
Market reaction: Oil continues to rise; risk assets also strengthen.
April 21 - Trump announces an indefinite extension of the ceasefire to leave room for negotiations. Iran refuses to attend talks in Islamabad and takes a hard line, stating that the next round of negotiations will only take place in Islamabad once Washington ends the blockade.
Market reaction: Gold rises, oil falls.
April 19–20 - On April 19, the Strait of Hormuz is completely closed within 72 hours; 13 oil tankers turn around, and the U.S. seizes an Iranian cargo ship. In the early hours of April 20, actual exchanges of fire break out in the Strait.
Market reaction: Oil prices jump immediately.
April 14 - Trump refuses to extend the ceasefire, previewing that "the next two days will be very eventful" and claiming that the war could end either with a deal or by "destroying Iran's capabilities" (leaning toward a deal).
Market reaction: Global capital flows back to the U.S. as a safe haven; the U.S. dollar index strengthens. Gold and oil rise.
April 12 - Islamabad talks end without result over the nuclear issue. Iran rejects the U.S. proposal for "joint management," insisting on retaining control of the Strait. Trump immediately announces a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. A "supply cut‑off crisis" emerges for global energy.
Market reaction: Stagflation trades kick off across the board. Oil rises; gold opens sharply lower then climbs; U.S. stocks weaken.
April 8 - A rift appears on the very first day of the U.S.–Iran ceasefire – Trump reneges on his promise in less than 24 hours, refusing to use Iran's "10‑point plan" as the basis for negotiations.
Market reaction: The brief peace expectation reverses instantly.
April 7 - Trump says that given Iran has agreed to fully reopen shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. agrees to suspend bombing. Iran immediately announces acceptance of the ceasefire, and Israel also agrees, setting April 10 as the date for talks in Islamabad.
Market reaction: The ceasefire news boosts market sentiment; U.S. stocks rally sharply.
